title: We Trust Fake Doctor Reviews More than Real Ones
paragraphs: When choosing a doctor, many people check online reviews written by other patients. However, a new study from Canada suggests that fake reviews may actually seem more believable to readers than genuine ones.

The study was led by Aishwarya Deep Shukla, an associate professor at Simon Fraser University's Beedie School of Business, and it was published in the journal Internet Research in 2026. The researchers analyzed 35,000 patient reviews that had been posted on an online platform in India between 2015 and 2017. The reviews covered a wide range of medical fields, from family medicine to dentistry and dermatology.

By taking advantage of a security flaw in the platform, the researchers were able to identify 8,313 fake reviews. These had been written by healthcare providers and clinic staff, some of whom had pretended to be patients.

The researchers then compared the fake reviews with the genuine ones. They found that the fake reviews tended to be longer and contained more details about symptoms, diagnoses, medicines and treatments. Surprisingly, these fake reviews also received more "helpful" votes from readers and scored higher on a measure of how trustworthy they seemed.

According to the researchers, fake reviews take advantage of a gap between what people want to read and what real patients are willing to share. While readers want detailed information, genuine patients rarely share such personal details publicly. For example, a real patient might simply write that a doctor was helpful, whereas a fake review might tell a detailed story.

Shukla also warned that artificial intelligence may make the problem worse. Although AI can help real patients write more complete and useful reviews, it can also help dishonest people produce detailed fake reviews more easily.
The researchers have recommended several measures to deal with the problem, such as only allowing reviews from people who have actually had appointments and introducing stronger moderation.

They also have advice for patients. People should read many reviews and look for common themes, be careful about reviews containing unusually detailed medical information and avoid dismissing doctors who have few reviews. They should also consider other sources of information, such as a doctor's qualifications and personal recommendations.
However, the study was based on reviews from only one country, posted several years ago, so further research is needed.
